item.title: [CBS News World] U.N. climate summit ends without deal after contentious fossil fuel debate
item.description:
COP31, the United Nations' annual climate conference, ended Sunday without a final agreement after days of contentious talks collapsed, mainly because of disputes between nations pushing to phase out fossil fuel use and others opposed to doing so.
The breakdown capped two weeks of negotiations in Antalya, Turkey, between delegations from nearly 200 countries. Their debates ran into overtime, becoming the longest COP summit in history, at a moment that U.N. officials and many scientists have called decisive for the trajectory of global warming and climate change.
The United States sent no representatives for the second year in a row, following the Trump administration's withdrawal from the 2015 Paris Agreement. That accord set a goal of limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels, a target that has anchored every U.N. climate summit since and that the world is now poised to overshoot.
Talks reached an impasse Sunday, as the European Union opposed a draft agreement that failed to mention fossil fuels and which, its delegates argued, placated countries that export them. They joined a group of smaller nations facing heightened threats of climate extremes and challenged oil producers, like Saudi Arabia, that staunchly rejected their views. The finale came after days of tense discussions over some of the core topics at issue during the summit, including whether to establish new rules and goals around transitioning away from coal, oil and natural gas in favor of renewable energy.
COP31 President Murat Kurum, who is Turkey's environmental minister, said in televised comments from Antalya on Sunday that a draft had not been adopted due to a lack of consensus. The conference rules require unanimous agreement to reach a deal, so even a single nation's dissent can derail the process.
"We have always emphasized that this process is one that respects the will of the parties. We did everything we could," Kurum said. "In the end, we did not impose this t...

item.description:

play video
Video Duration 47 minutes 26 seconds play-arrow
47:26
A look at how antibiotic overuse could fuel superbugs, killing eight million people annually by 2050.Read more
The challenges posed by antimicrobial resistance show where its impact is most acutely and tragically manifested: infant mortality in the developing world, specifically in sub-Saharan Africa. This film shows what these bland statistics mean in real terms to the health workers and families affected, following them as they struggle to fight this battle with low-tech solutions.
The Drugs Don’t Work follows the battle to the United Kingdom and examines how and why penicillin, the world’s most successful antibiotic, was invented. It then examines why pharmaceutical companies like GlaxoSmithKline are struggling to produce novel solutions to the problem of antimicrobial resistance (AMR).
The film also explores the cutting edge of academic research at British universities and hospitals supported by the power of the UK-based tech company DeepMind, and features academics and advocates who are devoting their lives to solving the problem. Returning to Africa, it shows how local innovation and the tools offered by the developed world are now saving lives and contributing to the global battle against AMR – an effort that could ultimately save millions of lives.Published On 22 Nov 202622 Nov 2026

item.title: [ABC News World] What to know about tear gas and reproductive health, as concerns are raised in France
item.description:
What to know about tear gas and reproductive health, as concerns are raised in France
French activists and lawmakers are demanding after recent protests that police stop using tear gas because of rising concerns about menstrual changes and reproductive health issuesBySYLVIE CORBET Associated PressNovember 22, 2026, 7:07 AM
Share
PARIS -- French activists and lawmakers are demanding after recent street protests that authorities suspend the use of tear gas to disperse crowds over concerns it's caused menstrual changes and other reproductive health problems, though scientists have not confirmed a medical connection.
The demands come after police used tear gas during student protests and demonstrations over the cost of living, some marred by violence. Some women reported painful cramps, unexpected bleeding and disrupted menstrual cycles after exposure, and an advocacy group says it has collected more than 10,000 complaints. Opposition lawmakers are seeking a ban and independent research into possible health effects.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez has rejected the calls, saying police use of tear gas is essential to crowd control as an alternative to using more dangerous weapons.
Here’s what is known — and what is not — about tear gas and reproductive health.
Tear gas grenades used by French police contain CS, a chemical irritant that affects the eyes, skin and respiratory tract. CS is a crystalline powder dispersed into the air as fine particles. Its effects depend upon how much is used and how long people are exposed to it.
Those exposed during the protests include peaceful demonstrators — including children, pregnant women and older people — and residents near the sites of protest marches.
Mélina Galland, 24, was working as an independent photographer during Oct. 17 protests in Paris that were marred by rioting and looting. She wore a double surgical mask along with a diving mask when tear gas grenades were fired.

item.title: [ABC News World] Okinawa celebrates restored Shuri Castle hall 7 years after fire
item.description:
Okinawa celebrates restored Shuri Castle hall 7 years after fire
Officials and residents in Okinawa have celebrated the restoration of Shuri Castle's main hall, marking a significant return of the island's cultural symbolByMARI YAMAGUCHI Associated PressNovember 22, 2026, 7:13 AM
Share
TOKYO -- Officials and residents in Okinawa celebrated the restoration of Shuri Castle's main hall on Sunday, its deep red exterior and dragon ornaments marking the return of a symbol of the island's heritage seven years after it was destroyed in a fire.
The fire on Oct. 31, 2019, destroyed several buildings at the castle complex in Naha, Okinawa’s prefectural capital, as it was hosting a festival. Firefighters struggled for nearly 12 hours to contain the blaze as it spread from building to building in strong winds. Investigators could not determine the cause but considered an electrical fault the likeliest explanation.
“The fire was a tremendous shock to the Okinawan people," Okinawa Gov. Genta Koja said at Sunday’s ceremony in the courtyard outside the main hall. "Seven years after the major loss, as we mark this milestone of the main hall restoration, I am deeply moved and delighted.”
The castle is a symbol of Okinawa’s cultural heritage dating to the Ryukyu Kingdom, which lasted about 450 years from 1429 until 1879, when Japan annexed the island.
It also represents Okinawa’s recovery from World War II. The castle burned down in 1945 during the Battle of Okinawa, which killed about 200,000 people, many of them civilians.
Koja thanked historians, artisans and other experts from across Japan who contributed to the restoration, as well as donors at home and abroad. He called for rebuilding the rest of the castle, saying the opening of the main hall, known as Seiden, is "not the end.”
The 2019 fire destroyed Seiden and two adjacent halls, as well as four nearby structures, while two other structures were heavily damaged.

item.description:
Air alert sounds hours after attack on Russia-bound ship in the Gulf of Finland
The governor of Kaliningrad says a rare air alert sounded in the Russian exclave near Poland and LithuaniaByThe Associated PressNovember 22, 2026, 7:14 AM
Share
KYIV, Ukraine -- A rare air alert sounded in Kaliningrad, the Russian exclave near Poland and Lithuania, according to the local governor, as claims circulated online of drone activity near a major naval base there.
The alert late Saturday in Kaliningrad came hours after a drone strike in the Gulf of Finland set fire to a Russian cargo ship bound for the region, which is a key base for Russia's Baltic Fleet. Finnish emergency services were still working to extinguish the blaze on Sunday.
Photos and video posted online show drone activity around the city of Baltiysk, where much of the fleet is stationed. But The Associated Press couldn't immediately verify the authenticity of the images.
According to local media, air raid sirens were heard in Kaliningrad for the first time since Russia’s all-out invasion of Ukraine on Feb. 24, 2022.
The Kaliningrad governor, Alexei Bezprozvannykh, said that “a suspicious object coming from the direction of Lithuania” triggered the alert in the Nemansky district near the Lithuanian border, about 170 kilometers (105 miles) northeast of Baltiysk.
On Russian Telegram channels, posts by users saying they were Baltiysk residents described air defenses working there during the night. They featured photos and videos of bright streaks against the night sky, with crackling sounds heard in the background.
Kaliningrad authorities on Sunday denounced as fake one photo, supposedly from Baltiysk, that showed clouds of smoke rising into the night sky, while an orange haze glowed on the horizon. They told Russian state media that the photo “had nothing to do with the region.”
As of Sunday morning, Russian authorities reported no casualties or damage in Kaliningrad.

item.description:

Finland says work is continuing on the Sparta II ship on SundayByHafsa KhalilPublished21 November 2026Updated 4 hours ago
Rescue and firefighting efforts are continuing for a Russian cargo vessel hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland, authorities have said.
The ship - the Sparta II - was bound for Russia's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad when it was hit on Saturday morning, before drifting into Finnish waters. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment.
Finland's Border Guard said on Sunday that work was ongoing to make sure the cargo ship did not sink but it was not aware of any danger to surrounding maritime traffic.
Water was still being used to douse the ship on Sunday, and Finland said Estonian and Russian assets were also involved in recovery work.
Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said two drones had been used in the strike, based on preliminary information, and there was "no threat" to the territory's supplies.
"War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said. "Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor."
The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and US governments.
The company says on its website that it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.
Finland's coast guard said it had been alerted to the attack at around 08:50 local time (06:50 GMT) on Saturday and that the cargo vessel had been located approximately 50km west of the island of Suursaari in the Gulf of Finland.
This prompted "temporary aviation and maritime restrictions" around the area, Finnish border officials said.

How South Korea tackles cheating on its college entrance examByJaroslav LukivPublished6 hours ago
South Korea's Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin has resigned over an exam cheating scandal that shocked the nation.
He said he took full responsibility for the confusion caused by last-minute measures aimed at stopping AI-assisted cheating during Thursday's annual college entrance exam, known as Suneung.
A week ago, the top scorer in the national tax accountancy exam admitted using a mini-camera, mobile phone and AI tools. This prompted officials to act urgently to detect hidden devices, including sending emergency alerts to every single mobile phone in the country.
The Suneung takes up to nine hours to complete, and it plays a big role in career trajectories of millions of South Koreans.
Image source, EPA/ShutterstockImage caption,
South Korean high school pupils in Daegu check their answers, a day after the annual college entrance exam
"As the minister in charge, I believe I cannot escape criticism that we failed to prepare in advance," Choi was quoted as saying on Sunday by South Korea's Yonhap's news agency.
"Now that the exam has concluded, I feel a deep sense of responsibility and am offering my resignation," the minister added.
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung - who has been calling for an overhaul of the current exam system - later accepted Choi's resignation.
The education ministry earlier said 111 candidates had been found with unauthorised smart devices during this year's Suneung, which was taken by about 500,000 students.
Concerns over academic dishonesty during the fiercely competitive exam had been brewing in recent weeks, after reports of candidates cheating with the help of AI devices.

Watch: Suspected drug lord 'El Chapo Isidro' transferred to Mexico's capitalByTara MewawallaPublished21 November 2026Updated 22 November 2026 01:25 GMT
A Mexican drug lord who was on the FBI's 10 most wanted list has been arrested following a shoot-out with Mexican authorities.
Fausto Isidro "Chapo Isidro" Meza Flores and seven others were detained by Mexican special forces in Guasave, Sinaloa on Friday, Mexico's defence secretariat said.
Seven suspects were killed in the operation, as were four members of the Mexican army who were travelling to reinforce security in Guasave, the secretariat added.
Meza Flores was wanted in Mexico on organised crime charges, while he has been accused of "flooding the US with fentanyl, cocaine, heroin and other deadly drugs" by the FBI. The US is seeking his extradition.
Mexico has stepped up efforts to tackle drug-related crime after coming under pressure from US President Donald Trump since he returned to the White House.
Meza Flores, the leader of the Meza Flores Organisation, also known as the Guasave Cartel, is thought to have been active in the drug trafficking trade since the 1990s but managed to evade authorities till now by maintaining a relatively low profile.
Image source, FBIImage caption,
Fausto Isidro "Chapo Isidro" Meza Flores was detained by Mexican special forces on Friday
Using US intelligence on his whereabouts, Mexican special forces descended on his location using "stealth and surprise", establishing a perimeter to prevent him from escaping and reinforcements arriving, Mexico's defence secretariat said.
However, they "came under attack from gunfire and explosives" before entering the property and arresting Meza Flores, the secretariat continued.

China commits to low-carbon electrification and help for others to improve
Exclusive: Countries at Cop31 are being urged to commit to deriving 35% of their energy from electricity by 2035
Cop31 live – latest updates
China is pushing for rapid electrification of its economy using low-carbon energy and will help other countries do the same, a senior member of the Chinese delegation at the Cop31 UN climate summit has said.
Wang Yi, a professor of energy and environment policy at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and a senior adviser to China’s government, said: “End-use electrification is a very clear direction. We can follow this direction while making the source of electricity clean. That’s the way to go forward.”
China is the biggest emitter of greenhouse gases by far, producing more than a quarter of the world’s total, so its push for electrification is significant.
At Cop31, countries are being asked to sign up to a target of deriving 35% of final energy consumption from electricity by 2035. Australia, the president of the negotiations, and the host nation Turkey have pushed the target and on Friday night Australia and China signed a joint statement endorsing the “35:35” goal.
But in the second draft text of the probable outcome from Cop31, released on Thursday, the electrification pledge was downgraded to one of a suite of voluntary options countries can take up to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions.

Trump threatens ‘tremendous penalties’ for US tech firms that build datacenters abroad
President gives wide-ranging White House press conference and says he has ‘fantastic relationships’ with Putin and Xi
Donald Trump threatened on Friday to impose “tremendous penalties” on American tech companies that build datacenters outside the US, though he gave no details and told reporters he had not yet informed his own officials about the plan.
In a discursive press conference from the White House briefing room, Trump also said he would “look into” the report that Iran had been planning to possibly detonate a “dirty bomb” in Washington DC, and backed JD Vance over comments the vice-president made blaming Republican midterm losses on the Iran war.
Trump also expounded on his friendship with the Russian president Vladimir Putin, whom he met alongside China’s Xi Jinping at the Apec summit on Thursday, adding he had “fantastic relationships” with both autocratic leaders.
At the White House, Trump told reporters he wanted datacenters built by US companies to stay on US soil.
“We’re not allowing datacenters to go into other countries, because China will take all of them, and we’re not allowing that to happen. And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try to do it,” he said.
He said Americans should welcome datacenters, and urged communities to extract concessions from developers, repeating a point he made before the midterms.
“You ought to take advantage of the datacenters. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but don’t shut them off,” he said.
“We want them to build it here.”

California’s coastal communities on alert as biggest waves in years hit state
Hazard warnings issued throughout week after powerful swells and waves of more than 9 metres recorded
Multiple coastal hazard warnings were issued this week across California as successive areas of low pressure generated powerful swells and large breaking waves for coastal communities. Beaches and piers were closed last weekend as large waves crashed into California’s coastline. Offshore National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration buoys recorded wave heights of greater than 30ft (9 metres) last Friday. The Monterey, California, buoy recorded a wave height of 34.1ft, which would make it the highest reading in 30 years.
Coastal warnings extended from last weekend through this week, with alerts extending until Friday night. Waves of 10-18ft are expected, with local sets of 18-22ft for San Luis Obispo county beaches and Santa Barbara county central coast beaches. These Pacific storm systems are also bringing unsettled conditions across the western US, with heavy rain, mountain snow, and strong winds through the coming days. Already, record-breaking rainfall affected San Fransisco on Wednesday, with heavy rain also causing 32,000 customers to lose power in Sacramento. Into this weekend, a further area of low pressure will bring considerable amounts of moisture for southern Oregon and northern California. By Sunday night, more than 100mm (4in) of rain is expected in places, with further snowfall for areas such as Donner Pass across the northern Sierra Nevada mountains.

Sarah Venter, founder of the Baobab Foundation, with one of the baobabs to be transported to Timbavati reserve in north-eastern South Africa. Photograph: Courtesy of Timbavati nature reserve
Race to replant five South African baobabs after export blocked
The trees, intended for an unnamed buyer in Georgia, were reportedly dug up without the necessary permits
Environmentalists in South Africa are racing to replant five centuries-old baobabs after the 20-tonne trees were dug up by an exporter, who tried to ship them thousands of miles to Georgia.
The baobabs arrived at a reserve in Timbavati, in north-eastern South Africa, on Wednesday, where they will be replanted and supported by cables to help them recover. The trees had been stranded at a warehouse in Durban since July, when they were intercepted by authorities who said they had been moved without the necessary permissions.
The department of forestry, fisheries and the environment confirmed the trees had been destined for Georgia but did not name the buyer.
The case echoes an episode in Kenya four years ago, when eight baobabs were uprooted to be exported to Shekvetili Dendrological Park, owned by Bidzina Ivanishvili, an influential Georgian billionaire and the country’s former prime minister. Ivanishvili has filled the park with ancient, giant trees from Georgia, transporting them by boat along the Black Sea.
The export of the Kenyan baobabs was initially blocked after an outcry by environmentalists, who condemned their export as biopiracy, but later allowed to go ahead.

item.title: [BBC China] This is a remarkable diplomatic moment for China's Xi - but it comes with pitfalls
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption,
Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are meeting for a historic trilateral summitByLaura BickerChina correspondent , Reporting fromShenzhenPublished19 November 2026
Xi Jinping will believe he has achieved something no other world leader could in securing a historic summit with Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump in Shenzhen.
For decades, Washington and its western allies shaped the world order.
Yet it is China that has orchestrated the remarkable diplomatic spectacle of three of the world's most powerful protagonists sitting around the table.
And surrounding it all is the futuristic display that is Shenzhen, with driverless cars cruising past as drones fly overhead and robots - literally - dance in the streets.
Ostensibly, this is an economic summit for Asia Pacific leaders. But for Xi, it is also a demonstration of China's grip on the global economy and world politics.
His country is no longer just reacting to decisions made in Washington, London or Brussels - instead Beijing is at the heart of conversations which are reshaping the international order.
But this meeting is not without its pitfalls for Xi as there are many things he does not appear keen to discuss with Putin and Trump.
Follow live updates: Trump, Xi and Putin hold historic meeting on Apec sidelines
Ukraine, the balancing act
First, China is not keen for the war in Ukraine, now well into its fifth year, to be on the agenda.
This is a delicate balancing act for Xi who is aware his relationship with Putin may damage China's connections in Europe. The EU is a key market, especially now when the Chinese economy is heavily relying on exports.
However Xi also doesn't want the war to end in a way that will destabilise Russia, a key ally and neighbour.
Beijing is still trying to maintain that it is neutral in this war and has repeatedly called for negotiations and a political settlement while avoiding condemnation of Russia&#x27...

View image in fullscreen
Seven countries in Africa expressly exempt husbands from prosecution for marital rape, including Côte d’Ivoire, Ethiopia and South Sudan. Photograph: Frank Dejongh/Unicef
One in four women globally unable to refuse sex within marriage, says UN
Almost half of women in west and central Africa cannot withhold consent, with girls worst affected, UNFPA finds
One in four women around the world have no power of consent if their husband or partner demands sex, according to a UN report.
In west and central Africa, almost half of women (45%) are not able to say no in their own marriage, while a third of women (33%) in east and southern Africa and in Arab states face the same predicament. In Latin America and the Caribbean, one in 10 women are not able to refuse sex, said the report by the UN Population Fund (UNFPA) published on Thursday.
Younger women and girls aged 15 to 19 had even less power to say no, compared with older women aged 45 to 49, according to analysis in the report of eight countries with comparable data (Angola, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kazakhstan, Malawi, Mali, Nigeria, Tajikistan and Zambia). The findings align with research showing adolescent girls endure very high rates of intimate partner violence.
“These are really sad figures,” said Jean-Paul Murunga, a lawyer with the global human rights organisation Equality Now. “Especially given that the continent of Africa as a whole has adopted the Maputo protocol, which sets [binding legal standards for] equality between women and men. We still have a lot of work to do to ensure women and girls benefit from these commitments.”
